title: Your first weekend
summary: Install the OS, give it a name, plug it in, reach it from the couch. Not a shopping trip.

start.body:
This is a weekend, not a shopping trip.

You already have the computer. The job: get it on, named, and reachable from the couch.

checklist.body:
You'll roughly do this:

1. Copy off anything you care about
2. Write the OS installer to a USB stick
3. Boot from the stick and install
4. Name the computer and create a user
5. Plug network
6. Find its address
7. Log in from your laptop (SSH)
8. Leave it on

One step at a time.

backup.body:
1. Backup anything you care about.

Copy photos or papers to a stick or another computer. Empty machine or already wiped? Skip.

choices.label: I need to copy stuff off first

copy-off.body:
Copy what you care about first.

Then, if it came from Marketplace, plan to wipe during install (the installer will erase the disk you pick).

usb.body:
2. Make a USB installer.

Download Ubuntu Server or Debian from the official site. Write the ISO with balenaEtcher, Rufus (Windows), or Ventoy.

An 8 GB stick is enough. What you'll see: a progress bar, then "ISO written" / success.

usb-stuck.body:
If you're stuck writing the USB:

• Try a different stick
• Re-download the ISO if the writer says checksum/verify failed
• On Windows, Rufus is common; on Mac, balenaEtcher

You should end with a stick that another computer might offer as a boot device.

boot.body:
3. Boot from the USB.

Power on and tap F12, F10, Esc, or F2 (varies by brand) to open the boot menu. Pick the USB stick — not the internal disk yet.

What you'll see: a text or graphical installer, not your old Windows desktop.

boot-stuck.body:
If it ignores the USB:

• Remake the stick
• Try another USB port (back of a desktop)
• In BIOS/UEFI, disable Secure Boot temporarily if the installer complains
• Make sure you picked the stick in the one-time boot menu

BIOS/UEFI = the tiny setup screen before the OS — blue/gray menus, mouse often doesn't work.

install.body:
Install to the internal disk. One disk is fine. Take the defaults.

You'll be asked language, keyboard, and which disk to erase. Double-check the disk name before confirming erase.

name.body:
4. Give it a name and a user.

Pick a hostname you'll remember: lab, closet, office. Create a username (not "admin" as the only tip — any simple name is fine).

Ubuntu: don't skip the SSH server checkbox if you see it — that lets you log in from the couch later.

net.body:
5. Plug ethernet if it has a port.

Wi‑Fi is fine; a cable drops fewer overnight connections. Finish the installer and reboot when it says so. Remove the USB when asked.

find.body:
6. Find its address.

On the lab computer (with a screen): run hostname -I and note the number like 192.168.1.50.

Or check your router's device list for the new name.

No fancy static IP yet — DHCP (automatic address) is fine.

find-stuck.body:
If you can't find an address:

• Confirm the cable lights blink
• On the lab box: ip a or hostname -I
• Reboot the router only as a last resort
• Same Wi‑Fi network as your laptop — guest Wi‑Fi often blocks device-to-device

ssh.body:
7. From the couch laptop:

```
ssh you@that-address
```

Swap you for the username you created, and that-address for the number.

First time: it asks to trust the host key — type yes. Then password (nothing shows as you type). Try hostname. Type exit to leave.

update.body:
8. Still connected, update packages:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
```

sudo = "do this as the administrator for one command." It will ask your password again. Let it finish; reboots if it asks.

leave.body:
9. Leave it on.

That is the lab. Skip Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, a new mini PC, 10G, and a UPS until it has been on a week without drama.

end.body:
Weekend checklist: installed, named, reachable, left on. Check each on your own machine; finishing this walkthrough does not verify it.

Next guided project: a deeper pass on SSH from the couch — troubleshooting refused connections and keys later.

tools.body:
Have nearby:

• USB stick (8 GB+)
• Another computer to download the ISO
• Screen + keyboard for the lab during install (borrow the TV HDMI if needed)
• Ethernet cable if you have one

reboot.body:
After install, the machine reboots into the new OS.

What you'll see on Server: a text login (username, then password). On Desktop: a graphical login.

Log in once at the machine before you chase SSH.

ssh-checkbox.body:
During Ubuntu Server install, a checkbox for OpenSSH / SSH server appears.

Check it. That installs the program that listens for your couch login.

Missed it? You can install later: sudo apt install openssh-server — covered again in SSH from the couch.

celebrate-week.body:
If apt upgrade finished and SSH worked once, the weekend succeeded.

Leave the box on. Notice it tomorrow. That boring uptime is the point.
